content.overview: Section 63 BNS codifies the substantive definition of Rape, directly succeeding Section 375 IPC. It defines four distinct actus reus modalities (penile penetration, non-penile object/body part insertion, bodily manipulation causing penetration, and oral-genital contact) committed under any of seven vitiating circumstances—including against her will, without consent, under fear of death/hurt, marital impersonation, cognitive incapacity/stupefaction, age under 18 years, or inability to communicate consent. Explanation 2 codifies the affirmative consent doctrine, while Exception 2 codifies the post-Independent Thought threshold preserving immunity only for wives aged 18 and above.

content.study:
I. LEGISLATIVE ARCHITECTURE & PRIMACY OF CHAPTER V
Section 63 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) forms the substantive cornerstone of sexual offences in Indian criminal jurisprudence. In the architectural reorganization of the Sanhita, Parliament placed offences against women and children in Chapter V ("Of Offences Against Woman and Child", Sections 63 to 99), deliberately giving them priority over offences against the State (Chapter VII) and general bodily offences (Chapter VI).
Section 63 directly succeeds Section 375 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, consolidating the radical paradigm shifts initiated by the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013 (post-Nirbhaya) and the landmark constitutional holding in Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017).

II. ACTUS REUS: THE FOUR MODALITIES UNDER SECTION 63
A man is said to commit rape if he engages in any of the four distinct physical acts set out in Section 63 clauses (a) to (d):
1. Clause (a) — Penile Penetration: Penetrates his penis, to any extent, into the vagina, mouth, urethra, or anus of a woman, or makes her do so with him or any other person.
   - "To any extent": The slightest degree of penetration suffices; rupture of the hymen or seminal emission is entirely unnecessary.
2. Clause (b) — Object or Non-Penile Bodily Insertion: Inserts, to any extent, any object or a part of the body (not being the penis) into the vagina, urethra, or anus of a woman, or makes her do so with him or any other person.
3. Clause (c) — Bodily Manipulation: Manipulates any part of the body of a woman so as to cause penetration into the vagina, urethra, anus, or any part of the body of such woman, or makes her do so with him or any other person.
4. Clause (d) — Oral-Genital Contact: Applies his mouth to the vagina, anus, or urethra of a woman, or makes her do so with him or any other person.

Anatomical Clarification (Explanation 1): "Vagina" statutorily includes labia majora. The statutory text expressly includes labia majora within “vagina”; avoid the broader claim that any contact, without applying the full statutory elements, necessarily establishes the offence.

III. MENS REA & THE SEVEN VITIATING CIRCUMSTANCES
The physical act becomes rape when committed under any of the seven statutory descriptions:
1. Description (i) — Against Her Will: Committed in active opposition to the victim's expressed volition.
2. Description (ii) — Without Her Consent: Committed in the absence of affirmative, voluntary agreement.
3. Description (iii) — Consent under Fear: With consent obtained by putting the woman, or any person in whom she is interested (such as her child or spouse), in fear of death or hurt.
4. Description (iv) — Marital Impersonation: With consent obtained when the man knows he is not her husband and consent is given because she believes he is another man to whom she is or believes herself to be lawfully married.
5. Description (v) — Unsoundness, Intoxication or Stupefaction: With consent given when, by reason of unsoundness of mind, intoxication, or the administration of any stupefying or unwholesome substance (personally or through another), she is unable to understand the nature and consequences of that to which she gives consent.
6. Description (vi) — Statutory Bar (Under 18 Years): With or without consent, when the girl is under eighteen years of age. Consent of a minor is non est and legally incapable of conferring immunity.
7. Description (vii) — Inability to Communicate: When the woman is unable to communicate consent (e.g. paralysis, vegetative state, shock, muteness, or catatonia).

IV. THE DOCTRINE OF AFFIRMATIVE CONSENT & EXPLANATION 2
Explanation 2 establishes the modern affirmative consent standard:
- "Consent means an unequivocal voluntary agreement when the woman by words, gestures or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication, communicates willingness to participate in the specific sexual act."
- Proviso on Absence of Physical Resistance: "Provided that a woman who does not physically resist to the act of penetration shall not by the reason only of that fact, be regarded as consenting to the sexual activity."
- Rejection of Submission as Consent: Submission under terror, intimidation, or passive resignation in the face of overpowering physical superiority does not constitute consent.

V. EXCEPTIONS & CONSTITUTIONAL HARMONIZATION
1. Exception 1 — Medical Procedure: A medical procedure or intervention does not constitute rape.
2. Exception 2 — Marital Rape Threshold: "Sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under eighteen years of age, is not rape."
   - Legislative Incorporation of Independent Thought: Under the old IPC Section 375 Exception 2, the age floor for marital exemption was 15 years. In Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 800, the Supreme Court struck down the exception for wives aged 15–18 as unconstitutional, harmonizing penal law with the POCSO Act, 2012. Parliament expressly codified this constitutional mandate into BNS Section 63 Exception 2 by fixing the threshold at 18 years.

VI. INTERPLAY WITH SECTION 69 BNS & SECTION 120 BSA
1. Distinguishing Rape from Section 69 BNS:
   - Where sexual intercourse occurs under a false promise of marriage or other deceitful means without violent coercion, the Supreme Court in Pramod Suryabhan Pawar (2019) and Anurag Soni (2019) held that consent is vitiated only if the promise was false ab initio. Under the BNS, Parliament separated this into a distinct substantive offence under Section 69 BNS.
2. Statutory Presumption under Section 120 BSA (old s. 114A IEA):
   - In prosecutions under Section 64(2) BNS, where sexual intercourse is proved and the prosecutrix deposes in court that she did not consent, the court shall presume absence of consent.

sections.heading: The legal rule
Substantive Definition & Four Actus Reus Modalities (Clauses a to d)
sections.body:
Section 63 BNS replaces Section 375 IPC, codifying the comprehensive definition of rape within Chapter V of the Sanhita.
Clause (a) penalizes penile penetration into the vagina, mouth, urethra, or anus to any extent; hymenal rupture or ejaculation is not required.
Clause (b) penalizes the insertion of any object or non-penile body part into the vagina, urethra, or anus.
Clause (c) covers bodily manipulation causing penetration, and Clause (d) penalizes oral-genital contact.
Explanation 1 clarifies that "vagina" statutorily includes labia majora, clarifying that “vagina” includes labia majora; the statutory ingredients and facts still determine whether the offence is established.

sections.heading: The Seven Vitiating Circumstances & Statutory Rape under 18 Years
sections.body:
Circumstance (i) covers acts against the will; Circumstance (ii) covers acts without consent.
Circumstance (iii) vitiates consent obtained through fear of death or hurt to the victim or any person in whom she is interested.
Circumstance (iv) addresses marital impersonation; Circumstance (v) addresses cognitive inability due to unsoundness, intoxication, or stupefying drugs.
Circumstance (vi) establishes absolute statutory liability: sexual acts with a girl under 18 years are rape regardless of consent.
Circumstance (vii) invalidates consent where the victim is physically or mentally unable to communicate consent.

sections.heading: The Affirmative Consent Standard & Proviso to Explanation 2
sections.body:
Explanation 2 defines consent as an unequivocal voluntary agreement communicated through words, gestures, or non-verbal conduct.
The Proviso to Explanation 2 enacts the vital safeguard that lack of physical resistance cannot be interpreted as consent.
The Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh (1996) discussed assessment of testimony in rape prosecutions; apply the judgment to its holding and facts rather than treating it as a substitute for the statutory ingredients.
Consent must be active, informed, contemporaneous, and specific to the particular sexual act.

sections.heading: Exceptions: Medical Intervention & Post-Independent Thought Marital Exception
sections.body:
Exception 1 protects bona fide medical procedures and healthcare interventions from criminal exposure.
Exception 2 codifies marital immunity only where the wife is eighteen years of age or older.
Codification of Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 800: Parliament eliminated the colonial 15-year marital exemption, making non-consensual or consensual intercourse with any minor wife under 18 an offence.
The constitutionality of the remaining marital rape exemption for adult wives remains sub judice before the Supreme Court of India.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Proof, Presumption (BSA s. 115) & Section 69 Delineation
sections.body:
Section 120 BSA applies only to a prosecution for rape under section 64(2) BNS, where sexual intercourse by the accused is proved and the woman states in court that she did not consent. Do not generalise this presumption to every rape prosecution.
The Two-Finger Test is strictly unconstitutional and prohibited (State of Jharkhand v. Shailendra Kumar Rai (2022)).
Distinction with Section 69 BNS: Consensual sexual intercourse induced by deceitful means or false promise of marriage is now tried under Section 69, preserving Section 63 for coercive non-consensual violations.
Section 531(2)(a) BNSS governs procedural transition: offences occurring prior to 1 July 2024 are charged under IPC Section 375/376; post-commencement acts are charged under BNS Section 63/64.

examples.title: Application of Section 63(b) and Explanation 1 — Insertion of Object
examples.body: Accused A corners a woman W in an office basement, immobilizes her, and forcibly inserts a glass bottle into her vagina, causing internal bleeding. Medical examination establishes lacerations to the labia majora and vaginal canal. A argues that since penile penetration did not take place, the offence of rape is not made out. Under Section 63(b) read with Explanation 1 BNS, inserting any object into the vagina (including labia majora) against her will constitutes rape. A is convicted of rape and sentenced under Section 64 BNS.

examples.title: Section 63 Description (vi) and Exception 2 — Interplay with Minor Wife
examples.body: H, aged 26, enters into a customary marriage with G, who is 16 years and 8 months of age, with the consent of her parents. H engages in sexual intercourse with G. In defence to a prosecution, H relies on Exception 2 to Section 63 claiming marital immunity. Under BNS Section 63 Exception 2, marital immunity is strictly conditioned on the wife "not being under eighteen years of age," codifying Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017). Because G is under 18, Exception 2 does not apply, and G’s consent is non est under Description (vi). H is guilty of rape under Section 63/64 BNS and aggravated sexual assault under POCSO.

hypotheticals.question: As Senior Counsel appearing for the prosecution, evaluate the liability of D under Section 63 BNS with particular reference to Circumstances (v) and (vii), Explanation 2, and the statutory proviso on physical resistance.
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Establishing the Physical Actus Reus:
   - Forensic DNA analysis confirms penile-vaginal penetration by D, establishing Section 63(a) BNS.
2. Vitiation of Consent under Description (v) and (vii):
   - Under Section 63(v), consent is vitiated when, by reason of the administration of any stupefying or unwholesome substance by the accused, the woman is unable to understand the nature and consequences of the act. Flunitrazepam toxicity is scientifically established.
   - Under Section 63(vii), the physical paralysis and semi-consciousness rendered V unable to communicate consent.
3. The Affirmative Consent Doctrine & Proviso to Explanation 2:
   - Explanation 2 requires an unequivocal voluntary agreement communicated through words, gestures, or non-verbal conduct. Silence or cognitive impairment cannot constitute communication of willingness.
   - The statutory proviso explicitly commands that a woman who does not physically resist shall not, by reason only of that fact, be regarded as consenting. D’s reliance on absence of resistance is legally untenable.
4. Presumption of Absence of Consent:
   - Under Section 120 BSA, once sexual intercourse is proved and V deposes that she did not consent, the court shall presume lack of consent. D has produced no evidence capable of rebutting this statutory presumption.

misconceptions.trap: Believing that absence of physical injury or lack of physical struggle implies consent.
misconceptions.correction: The Proviso to Explanation 2 of Section 63 BNS expressly dictates that a woman who does not physically resist shall not by reason only of that fact be regarded as consenting. Passive submission under fear or trauma is not consent.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming marital immunity under Exception 2 shields a husband where the wife is 16 or 17 years old.
misconceptions.correction: Following Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 800, Parliament codified the age floor at eighteen years in Exception 2. Sexual intercourse with a wife under 18 is statutory rape under Section 63(vi).

misconceptions.trap: Relying on the "two-finger test" or past sexual history to challenge the victim’s credit.
misconceptions.correction: The Supreme Court in State of Jharkhand v. Shailendra Kumar Rai (2022) declared the two-finger test illegal and unconstitutional. Furthermore, Section 53A of the Indian Evidence Act (now Section 52 BSA) strictly bars evidence of the victim’s character or prior sexual experience to prove consent.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Appellate Written Submissions: Vitiation of Consent under Section 63 BNS and Affirmative Consent Standard
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
MAY IT PLEASE YOUR LORDSHIPS:

1. LOCUS OF THE PROVISION & CHARGING MATRIX:
The appellant stands convicted of Rape under Section 63 punishable under Section 64(1) BNS. It is submitted that the conviction is legally sound and calls for no interference.

2. ESTABLISHMENT OF ACTUS REUS UNDER SECTION 63(a) READ WITH EXPLANATION 1:
The medical deposition of the gynaecologist (PW-3) and the forensic DNA report (Ex. P-7) confirm penile penetration. Under Section 63(a) read with Explanation 1, penetration to any extent into the vagina (including labia majora) completes the actus reus. Rupture of the hymen or physical trauma is not a legal prerequisite.

3. AFFIRMATIVE CONSENT STANDARD UNDER EXPLANATION 2 & PROVISO:
The defense contends that the prosecutrix did not raise an immediate hue and cry and bore no marks of physical struggle. This contention runs directly counter to positive statutory law:
(a) Explanation 2 to Section 63 BNS statutorily defines consent as "an unequivocal voluntary agreement when the woman by words, gestures or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication, communicates willingness to participate in the specific sexual act."
(b) The Proviso to Explanation 2 commands: "Provided that a woman who does not physically resist to the act of penetration shall not by the reason only of that fact, be regarded as consenting to the sexual activity."
(c) The Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh (1996) 2 SCC 384 and State of U.P. v. Chhotey Lal (2011) 2 SCC 550 held that absence of injuries on the prosecutrix or absence of physical struggle cannot give rise to an inference of consent, particularly when the victim is subjected to intimidation or overpowering duress.

4. APPLICATION OF SECTION 120 BSA PRESUMPTION:
Once the physical act of sexual intercourse is admitted or proved, and the prosecutrix deposes on oath that she did not consent, Section 115 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 mandates that the Court shall presume absence of consent. The appellant has produced no evidence capable of rebutting this mandatory statutory presumption.

5. TOTAL UNCONSTITUTIONALITY OF TWO-FINGER TEST & PAST SEXUAL HISTORY:
The appellant’s attempt to cross-examine PW-1 regarding prior relationship history is barred by Section 52 BSA (old s. 53A IEA). Furthermore, any reliance on hymenal examination is barred by the definitive ruling in State of Jharkhand v. Shailendra Kumar Rai (2022) SCC OnLine SC 1494.

6. CONCLUSION & PRAYER:
All essential ingredients of Section 63 BNS are proved beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal is devoid of merit and ought to be dismissed.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Comprehensive appellate submissions establishing actus reus, affirmative consent doctrine under Explanation 2, statutory presumption under BSA s. 115, and exclusion of two-finger test.

cases.name: Independent Thought v. Union of India
cases.holding: The Supreme Court struck down the exception protecting sexual intercourse with a married girl child between 15 and 18 years, holding it unconstitutional and violative of Articles 14, 15, and 21. Parliament directly incorporated this judgment into BNS Section 63 Exception 2, establishing that sexual intercourse with any wife under 18 years constitutes rape.

cases.name: State of Jharkhand v. Shailendra Kumar Rai
cases.holding: Reiterated the absolute ban on the regressive and traumatizing "two-finger test" (per vaginum examination) on rape survivors, holding that a woman’s sexual history has no bearing on whether she gave consent, and directing that conducting the test constitutes criminal misconduct.

cases.name: State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh
cases.holding: Established that the testimony of a rape prosecutrix is equivalent to that of an injured witness; if it inspires confidence, conviction can rest entirely upon her sole uncorroborated testimony. Delay in lodging FIR in sexual offences is natural due to social stigma.

cases.name: Pramod Suryabhan Pawar v. State of Maharashtra
cases.holding: Distinguished between a false promise to marry made from the inception with no intention of fulfilling it (vitiating consent under misconception of fact) and a genuine breach of promise due to subsequent circumstances. This doctrinal distinction led Parliament to codify Section 69 BNS as a distinct offence.

cases.name: Tukaram v. State of Maharashtra
cases.holding: The infamous Mathura case where the Supreme Court erroneously inferred consent from lack of physical resistance, sparking nationwide legal reform that culminated in the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 1983, the statutory definition of affirmative consent, and statutory presumptions.

examTips: Always cite Section 63 BNS for the substantive definition of rape and Section 64 BNS for the penal sanctions; never conflate definition with punishment.
Carefully distinguish between Section 63 (violent/non-consensual sexual offences) and Section 69 BNS (sexual intercourse by deceitful means or false promise of marriage).
Memorize the four actus reus limbs (clauses a to d) and the seven vitiating descriptions (clauses i to vii).
Highlight the constitutional incorporation of Independent Thought (2017) in Exception 2 fixing the marital exception floor strictly at 18 years.
Under Section 531(2)(a) BNSS, offences committed prior to 1 July 2024 are charged under Section 375/376 IPC, while post-commencement offences are charged under Section 63/64 BNS.

examFrameworks.question: Structured Chamber Brief: Section 63 BNS Substantive Elements and Consent Analysis
steps: Place Section 63 in Chapter V ("Of Offences Against Woman and Child") and highlight legislative primacy.
Deconstruct the four physical actus reus limbs under clauses (a), (b), (c), and (d).
Analyze which of the seven vitiating descriptions (i to vii) is attracted by the facts.
Apply Explanation 1 (vagina includes labia majora) and Explanation 2 (affirmative consent and lack of physical resistance).
Examine Exception 1 (medical intervention) and Exception 2 (marital exception floor at 18 years).
Evaluate evidentiary proof under Section 120 BSA presumption (limited to prosecutions under BNS section 64(2)) and State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh.
State procedural and sentencing linkage with Section 64 BNS and Section 531 BNSS transitional rules.

examFrameworks.question: Appellate Submissions: Rebutting Defense of Consent and Proving Vitiation under Section 63
steps: Formulate the issue: whether sexual acts were accompanied by affirmative consent under Explanation 2.
Demonstrate that lack of physical injury or protest does not establish consent under the Proviso to Explanation 2.

Invoke statutory presumption under Section 120 BSA only where the prosecution is under BNS section 64(2), sexual intercourse by the accused is proved, and the woman states in court that she did not consent.
Exclude defense cross-examination on past sexual history under Section 52 BSA and Shailendra Kumar Rai.
Conclude with the prayer affirming conviction under Section 63 read with Section 64 BNS.

answerSkeleton: Introduction — Section 63 BNS, Chapter V ("Of Offences Against Woman and Child"), replacing Section 375 IPC.
Actus Reus — Four modalities: penile penetration (cl. a), object/body part insertion (cl. b), manipulation (cl. c), oral contact (cl. d).
Circumstances — Seven vitiating descriptions: against will, without consent, fear, marital impersonation, cognitive incapacity, under 18, inability to communicate.
Consent Doctrine — Explanation 2 (affirmative voluntary agreement) and Proviso (lack of physical resistance is not consent).
Exceptions — Medical procedure (Exc. 1) and Marital exception for wives 18+ (Exc. 2, Independent Thought).
Evidentiary Rules — Presumption under BSA s. 115, sole testimony rule (Gurmit Singh), prohibition of two-finger test (Shailendra Kumar Rai).
Transition & Punishment — Charged with Section 64 BNS; IPC concordance for pre-1 July 2024 acts under BNSS s. 531.
revisionPoints: Section 63 BNS defines Rape; Section 64 BNS provides the punishment.
Explanation 1 includes labia majora within the definition of vagina.
Explanation 2 defines consent affirmatively; the proviso explicitly rules out inferring consent from absence of physical resistance.
Exception 2 protects marital relations only where the wife is 18 years or older, directly codifying Independent Thought v. Union of India.
Section 69 BNS now specifically governs sexual intercourse by deceitful means (including false promise to marry), separating it from Section 63.

learningObjectives: Master the substantive definition of rape across all four physical acts under BNS s. 63.
Analyze the seven non-consensual circumstances including absence of consent, fear, and age under eighteen.

enhancement.definition: BNS s. 63 defines rape as a man committing any of the four enumerated acts (penetration of penis into vagina, mouth, urethra, or anus; insertion of objects or other body parts; manipulation of body parts; or application of mouth) with a woman under any of seven circumstances: against her will, without her consent, with consent obtained by fear of death/hurt, with consent under false belief of marriage, with consent during unsoundness/intoxication, with or without consent when under eighteen years of age, or when unable to communicate consent.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Rape is a supreme bodily violation criminalizing non-consensual sexual acts. The law broadens the actus reus beyond penile-vaginal penetration, enforces affirmative unequivocal consent, and establishes an absolute age of consent at eighteen years.
statutoryFramework: Chapter V — Of Offences against Women and Children, BNS s. 63 (corresponding to IPC s. 375).
Actus Reus (Clauses a–d): Penile penetration, insertion of objects/non-penile parts, manipulation, application of mouth.

Circumstances (Clauses 1–7): Against will; without consent; consent under fear of death/hurt; false belief of husband; unsoundness/intoxication; under eighteen years of age; unable to communicate consent.
Explanation 1: Penetration to any extent is sufficient.
Explanation 2: Consent means unequivocal voluntary agreement by words or non-verbal communication; mere absence of physical resistance is NOT consent.
Exception 1: Medical procedure or intervention in good faith.
Exception 2: Sexual intercourse by a man with his wife, the wife not being under eighteen years of age.
essentialIngredients: The man committed any of the four acts enumerated in clauses (a) to (d).
The act was committed under any of the seven enumerated circumstances.
The woman was not the man's wife aged eighteen or above.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 63 is the cornerstone of criminal sexual offences. Following modern reforms, the definition encompasses four specific physical intrusions: (a) penile penetration; (b) inserting any object or any part of the body not being the penis into the vagina, urethra, or anus; (c) manipulating any part of the woman's body so as to cause penetration; and (d) applying the mouth to the woman's vagina, anus, or urethra. Consent is defined strictly under Explanation 2 as an unequivocal voluntary agreement; silence, passive submission, or the absence of physical injuries does not infer consent. For any girl under eighteen years of age, consent is completely immaterial (statutory rape).
examples: Teaching example (Absence of physical resistance): An assailant corners a woman in an isolated office and threatens to ruin her career if she does not submit. She remains completely silent and passive out of shock and distress. Under Explanation 2, passive non-resistance does not constitute consent; s. 63 is satisfied.

Teaching example (Under eighteen years): An adult man engages in consensual sexual intercourse with a seventeen-year-old girl. Even though she gave full express consent, s. 63 applies because consent of a female under eighteen is void in law.
distinctions: Rape (s. 63) vs Deceitful intercourse (s. 69): Section 63 applies where consent is vitiated under the seven statutory circumstances; Section 69 specifically penalizes sexual intercourse obtained by deceitful means such as false promise to marry.
Submission vs Unequivocal agreement: Passive submission under duress or shock is not legal consent under Explanation 2.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who engaged in sexual acts with a woman who was rendered intoxicated by drugs can claim the defence of consent.
Rule: Under BNS s. 63 (Fifthly), an act committed with consent where the woman is unable to understand the nature and consequences due to intoxication constitutes rape.
Application: Medical reports prove high blood-alcohol and narcotic presence, rendering the victim incapable of rational judgment.
Conclusion: Consent was legally void; the offence of rape under s. 63 is complete.
